# Hypoparathyroidism

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Thyroid and parathyroid gland disorders > Hypoparathyroidism*

[Original Article Link](/library/Sg0yu2)

---

## Summary

Hypoparathyroidism is an endocrinological disorder characterized by <u>parathyroid hormone</u> (<u>PTH</u>) deficiency. The most common cause of hypoparathyroidism is damage or injury to the <u>parathyroid glands</u> during <u>anterior</u> neck <u>surgery</u>, which leads to impaired <u>PTH</u> synthesis and/or secretion. Other causes include genetic conditions and autoimmune or infiltrative <u>parathyroid gland</u> destruction. Congenital disorders affecting <u>parathyroid gland</u> development typically manifest in childhood. Pseudohypoparathyroidism manifests similarly to hypoparathyroidism but is caused by resistance to <u>PTH</u> rather than insufficient <u>hormone</u> levels. <u>Hypocalcemia</u> is the primary manifestation of both hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathyroidism, and can cause symptoms ranging from muscle cramps to <u>seizures</u> or <u>heart failure</u>. Chronic hypoparathyroidism can cause <u>basal ganglia</u> calcifications (resulting in <u>extrapyramidal disorders</u>), <u>cataracts</u>, and skeletal and dental abnormalities. The presence of <u>hypocalcemia</u> and concurrent low (or inappropriately normal) <u>PTH</u> levels on two separate occasions ≥ 2 weeks apart confirms the diagnosis. Management typically includes correcting <u>hypocalcemia</u> through <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation and monitoring for complications. <u>PTH</u> replacement therapy may be indicated in selected patients.

---

## Etiology

* Postoperative: most commonly occurs as the result of accidental injury to parathyroids (or their blood supply) during <u>thyroidectomy</u>, <u>parathyroidectomy</u>, or radical <u>neck dissection</u>

* Autoimmune: : second most common cause

* Nonautoimmune destruction

* Infiltration of <u>parathyroid gland</u>

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Hemochromatosis</u>

* <u>Granulomas</u>

* <u>Metastases</u>

* Radiation-induced destruction

* Gram-negative <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Toxic shock syndrome</u>

* <u>HIV infection</u>

* Congenital

* <u>Parathyroid gland</u> <u>aplasia</u> or <u>hypoplasia</u> (DiGeorge syndrome)

* <u>PTH</u> <u>gene</u> mutation

* <u>Autosomal dominant</u> <u>hypocalcemia</u>

* Functional hypoparathyroidism: caused by <u>hypermagnesemia</u> or <u>hypomagnesemia</u> (reversible)  [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)





> [!TIP]
> Consider hypoparathyroidism in patients who present with <u>hypocalcemia</u> after <u>surgery</u> for <u>head and neck cancer</u>, e.g., <u>thyroidectomy</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

---

## Clinical features

### Acute manifestations [[3]](/library/ww1hOQ0)



* <u>Clinical features of hypocalcemia</u>, e.g.: 

* Neurological: <u>tetany</u>, <u>laryngospasm</u>, <u>seizures</u>

* Cardiac: <u>arrhythmias</u>




> [!TIP]
> The presence of the <u>Chvostek sign</u> or <u>Trousseau sign</u> in response to provocative maneuvers may help to identify latent <u>tetany</u> in patients with asymptomatic <u>hypocalcemia</u>. [[4]](/library/PiYW7K)




### Chronic manifestations




* <u>Extrapyramidal disorders</u> 

* <u>Parkinsonism</u>

* <u>Dystonia</u>

* <u>Hemiballismus</u>

* <u>Choreoathetosis</u>

* <u>Oculogyric crises</u>

* <u>Dementia</u>

* Ocular disease

* <u>Cataracts</u>

* <u>Keratoconjunctivitis</u>

* Skeletal manifestations

* Increased <u>bone mineral density</u>

* <u>Osteosclerosis</u>

* Dental abnormalities

* Dental <u>hypoplasia</u>

* Failure of <u>tooth</u> eruption

* Defective root formation

* Cutaneous manifestations: dry, puffy, coarse <u>skin</u>

## Diagnosis

Assess for hypoparathyroidism in patients with confirmed <u>hypocalcemia</u> and all patients after <u>total thyroidectomy</u>.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)




#### Diagnostic confirmation




Both results must be present on two separate occasions, ≥ 2 weeks apart.  [[5]](/library/Lybwfw)




* Serum <u>calcium</u>: below the <u>LLN</u>

* Serum intact <u>PTH</u>: low or inappropriately normal





> [!TIP]
> <u>Calcium</u> levels respond to changes in <u>PTH</u> levels within minutes. To ensure accurate results, perform <u>calcium</u> and <u>PTH</u> studies concurrently.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Severe hypocalcemia</u> is a <u>medical emergency</u>. Do not wait for confirmation of the underlying etiology to initiate <u>treatment of hypocalcemia</u>.




![Calcium correction for hypoalbuminemia](media/pqd5s6w9f42eo43ct2ytqblm.jpg)

Calcium correction for hypoalbuminemia




#### Additional studies [[6]](/library/YG1nBR0)




The following findings help support the diagnosis, monitor for complications, and guide management.




* Blood tests

* <u>Phosphate</u>: typically elevated

* <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> (<u>1,25[OH]2D</u>): normal or low (due to reduced renal production)  [[7]](/library/gG1FAR0)

* <u>25-hydroxyvitamin D</u> (<u>25[OH]D</u>): normal

* <u>Magnesium</u>: to assess for <u>functional hypoparathyroidism</u>

* <u>Creatinine</u>: Elevated levels suggest renal dysfunction, which is a common complication.

* Urine <u>Ca/Cr clearance ratio</u>: typically elevated

* <u>Genetic testing</u>: Obtain for patients with nonsurgical hypoparathyroidism and any of the following

* Age < 40 years

* <u>Family history</u> of nonsurgical hypoparathyroidism

* Syndromic pattern (e.g., features of <u>autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1</u>)





### Renal imaging [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)




* Assess for <u>nephrocalcinosis</u> and <u>nephrolithiasis</u> at the time of diagnosis.

* Options include CT abdomen or <u>renal ultrasound</u>.





### Postthyroidectomy assessment [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)




* Measure serum <u>PTH</u> levels 12–24 hours after <u>total thyroidectomy</u>.

* Interpretation [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)

* <u>PTH</u> < 10 pg/mL: Permanent hypoparathyroidism is possible.

* <u>PTH</u> > 10 pg/mL: Permanent hypoparathyroidism is unlikely.

---

## Differential diagnoses

See “<u>Interpretation of laboratory findings in hypocalcemia</u>.”




### Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A)




* Definition: end-organ (i.e., bones and <u>kidneys</u>) resistance to <u>parathyroid hormone</u> (<u>PTH</u>) despite sufficient <u>PTH</u> synthesis due to a defective <u>G<sub>s</sub> protein</u> α subunit

* Inheritance

* <u>Autosomal dominant</u>

* Inherited from the mother (<u>GNAS gene</u> <u>imprinting</u>)

* Pathophysiology: mutations in GNAS1 → impaired encoding of α subunit → missing activation of <u>adenylate cyclase</u> when <u>PTH</u> binds to G<sub>s</sub> → resistance to <u>PTH</u> in <u>kidney</u> and <u>bone tissue</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Albright hereditary osteodystrophy</u> (<u>AHO</u>)

* Round face

* <u>Short stature</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Brachydactyly</u> of the 4<sup>th</sup> and 5<sup>th</sup> fingers

* <u>Intellectual disability</u>

* Subcutaneous ossifications

* Symptoms related to low <u>calcium</u> and high <u>phosphate</u> levels

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Numbness, <u>tetany</u>

* <u>Cataracts</u>

* Dental problems

* Diagnostics

* Persistent <u>hypocalcemia</u> despite ↑ <u>PTH</u> levels

* ↑ <u>Phosphate</u> levels





### Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism




* Definition: extremely rare condition that mimics PHP1A but without end-organ resistance to <u>PTH</u>

* Inheritance

* <u>Autosomal dominant</u>

* Defective <u>G<sub>s</sub> protein</u> α subunit is inherited from the father (<u>GNAS gene</u> <u>imprinting</u>).

* The normal <u>allele</u> from the mother allows for maintaining the responsiveness of the <u>kidneys</u> to <u>PTH</u>.

* Clinical features: <u>Albright hereditary osteodystrophy</u>

* Diagnostics: normal <u>calcium</u>, <u>PTH</u>, and <u>phosphate</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

All patients should receive conventional therapy with <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation. Refer to an endocrinologist for definitive management.




### <u>Treatment of hypocalcemia</u> [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Indications for urgent <u>calcium repletion</u> include:

* <u>Severe hypocalcemia</u>

* <u>Symptoms of hypocalcemia</u>

* <u>ECG findings of hypocalcemia</u>

* Agents

* <u>Calcium gluconate</u> OR <u>calcium</u> <u>chloride</u>

* See “<u>Repletion regimens for hypocalcemia</u>” for dosages.

* Disposition: hospital admission for <u>cardiac monitoring</u> if IV <u>calcium repletion</u> is indicated





### Pharmacotherapy [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)[[7]](/library/gG1FAR0)




Therapeutic regimens are adjusted and dosages titrated to achieve target serum levels.




* <u>Vitamin</u> and mineral supplementation: indicated for all patients 

* <u>Calcium</u> (e.g., <u>calcium carbonate</u> or <u>calcium</u> <u>citrate</u>): target serum <u>calcium</u> at or slightly below the <u>LLN</u>

* <u>Vitamin D</u> (e.g., <u>cholecalciferol</u>, <u>ergocalciferol</u>, or <u>calcitriol</u>): to maintain serum <u>25[OH]D</u> level above 20–30 ng/mL [[7]](/library/gG1FAR0)

* <u>Magnesium</u> (e.g., <u>magnesium</u> oxide): to maintain normal serum <u>magnesium</u> levels

* <u>PTH</u> replacement therapy (subcutaneous recombinant human <u>PTH</u> 1–84)

* Indicated in patients with inadequate serum <u>calcium</u> control and/or adverse effects from conventional therapy

* Can be given in addition to, or instead of, conventional therapy

* Decreases <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation needs, and reduces serum <u>phosphate</u> and urine <u>calcium</u> levels

* <u>Thiazide diuretics</u>

* Reduce <u>hypercalciuria</u>; may prevent <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>

* Require adherence to a <u>low-sodium diet</u> and careful monitoring of blood pressure and <u>electrolytes</u>





### Monitoring [[1]](/library/TG16AR0)




Regular follow-up studies facilitate early identification of complications.




* Patients on stable therapy: serum <u>creatinine</u>, <u>calcium</u>, <u>magnesium</u>, and <u>phosphate</u> levels every 3–12 months

* Within days of a significant change in treatment: serum <u>calcium</u> level
